questions.q: Every catalog item, category, and flow built in this lesson has to trace back to what?
options: A one-off idea that seemed useful during the build
A line in Lesson 14's written, approved Phase 1 scope document
Whatever the development team finds fastest to build
The full enterprise rollout, built all at once
questions.explain: Nothing in this build is invented fresh -- it has to trace back to Lesson 14's approved scope, and anything not in that scope stays out.

questions.q: How does the shared catalog variable set resolve the St. Catherine's/Lakeshore/Prairie View category conflict from Lesson 13?
options: It forces all three systems onto St. Catherine's detailed multi-tier scheme
It ignores the conflict and uses free text for every request
It fixes five shared top categories corporately, with a Subcategory field that filters to each caller's own domain-specific list
It gives each domain a completely separate catalog item with no shared structure at all
questions.explain: The Request Category list is fixed corporately (Hardware, Software, Access, Facilities-Adjacent, Other); the Subcategory field underneath it filters to whichever domain the caller belongs to, preserving each system's own level of detail.

questions.q: Why does this lesson build one domain-aware Flow Designer flow instead of three near-identical flows, one per hospital system?
options: Flow Designer technically cannot support more than one active flow at a time
Three separate flows would be faster to build and easier to maintain
One flow that reads the caller's own domain is less duplication to maintain and is the version that actually proves the architecture holds up consistently across all three domains
Domain Separation requires a separate flow per domain by platform design
questions.explain: Three near-duplicate flows is exactly the kind of duplication this track's Flow Designer course warned against, and it risks drifting out of sync between domains over time.

questions.q: In `ServiceDeskRouting.getAssignmentGroupForCaller`, what happens if no assignment-group mapping exists for the caller's domain?
options: The script throws an unhandled error and the flow fails
It falls back to the corporate default Service Desk group rather than guessing at a domain-specific one
It assigns the request to the caller's own manager instead
It silently assigns the request to a randomly chosen domain's group
questions.explain: The function fails safe to a documented default group property instead of guessing -- an explicit fallback, not a silent failure.

questions.q: In `ServiceDeskApprovals.getApproverForAccessRequest`, why does the function return `null` when the requester's manager is in a different domain?
options: Because managers are never allowed to approve any requests on this platform
Because it fails closed -- it refuses to route an approval across a domain boundary it can't confirm, rather than guessing at an approver
Because cross-domain management structures are technically impossible to represent
Because `null` always means the request is automatically approved
questions.explain: That's the "fail closed" principle this lesson applies to approval routing: when the domain check doesn't hold, the subflow refuses to guess rather than risk an approval crossing a domain boundary.
